extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, and practitioners litigating or advising on APA notice-and-comment and good cause issues
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative framework and doctrinal guidance for judicial review of agency invocations of the APA good cause exception to notice-and-comment rulemaking; proposes that courts apply no deference (de novo review) and explains how to apply that standard in typical factual contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory good cause test (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(3)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may forgo notice-and-comment when 'the agency for good cause finds' that 'notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling statutory text; courts must assess agency invocations against these three statutory predicates (impracticable, unnecessary, contrary to the public interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative-history-backed narrowness
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA’s drafters intended the good cause exception to be 'reserved for rare instances' and warned it was not an 'escape clause'; early materials emphasized narrow construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations should respect the drafters’ insistence that the exemption be narrow; courts should be mindful of the legislative history that links each statutory term to discrete justifications (e.g., 'impracticable' -> need for quick action; 'unnecessary' -> minor/technical amendment; 'contrary to the public interest' -> preventing interference with statutory duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to make and publish a supported finding
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'true and supported or supportable' finding of necessity (good cause) must be made and published when the exception is invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should provide contemporaneous justification within the rulemaking record; absence of explanation or contemporaneous support undermines the invocation. Courts should look for a published statement of reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency / urgency criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause may be warranted where quick agency action is necessary to address an urgent threat to public safety or other compelling time-sensitive interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic example: post-September 11 FAA security measures. Courts assess whether the asserted urgency is genuine, fact-supported, and not self-created; mere asserted concern is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability focused on need for quick action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Impracticable' was meant to focus on the need for quick action—circumstances where delay to allow notice-and-comment would prevent the agency from fulfilling its duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should evaluate whether the delay inherent in notice-and-comment would make the agency unable to meet statutory responsibilities or avert harm; courts should test that claim against the record and agency conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnecessary: minor or technical amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unnecessary' was intended to cover instances such as minor or merely technical amendments where notice-and-comment would add no meaningful public participation benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for narrow, noncontroversial, clerical, or purely technical changes; courts should be attentive to whether the change truly is minor in scope and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrary-to-public-interest justification
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Contrary to the public interest' addresses situations where providing advance notice would undermine the public interest—e.g., would prevent the agency from performing statutory duties or would enable harmful strategic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should scrutinize agency claims that notice would be detrimental, including evidence that public notice would allow actors to frustrate regulatory objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of statutory deadlines and implicit congressional waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: In some contexts courts examine whether statutory deadlines or Congress’s structure implicitly authorize expedited action or waiver of notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider the statutory scheme and whether Congress intended or reasonably anticipated expedited action; but implicit waiver is not automatic and must be carefully evaluated (courts have rejected simplistic implicit-waiver claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny for agency-created emergencies or delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should treat agency invocations of urgency skeptically when the agency's own delay or inaction produced or undermined the claimed emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency's protracted delay between awareness and action weakens urgency claims; courts should weigh the agency's conduct (e.g., seven-month delay in SORNA example) when assessing good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of reliance interests and retroactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Presumption against retroactivity is relevant; courts consider reliance interests when agencies use good cause to make rules retroactive or to change settled expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where rules affect reliance interests, courts should be reluctant to accept retroactivity rationales absent strong record support; statutory clear-statement principles apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of strategic-action claims (risk that notice enables evasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies sometimes argue that advance notice would permit sophisticated actors to take strategic or evasive actions that would frustrate statutory objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should analyze, on the record, whether a comment period would realistically enable strategic evasion and whether preemptive action is necessary to prevent such harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity across rule types
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause has been invoked for many forms of action—interim final rules, direct final rules, suspensions of the APA’s 30-day delay, emergency rules, and minor clerical fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The particular procedural posture matters; courts apply the statutory predicates to the factual context, recognizing the 'exceedingly factbound' nature of the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpromulgation comment acceptance and harmless-error treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts treat omission of notice-and-comment as harmless if agencies accept and respond to comments after promulgation, minimizing the consequences of improper good cause claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice varies; courts should be cautious that postpromulgation comments do not become a way to avoid the statutory process—harmless-error treatment should not swallow the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow-construction and reluctance to countenance the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts repeatedly state the exception must be 'narrowly construed and reluctantly countenanced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial posture should favor notice-and-comment unless the record and statutory text clearly justify deviation; judges should avoid expansive readings that turn the exception into an 'escape clause.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review: de novo (no deference) to agency assertions of good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should afford no deference to agency assertions that good cause exists and should review those assertions de novo rather than under an arbitrary-and-capricious (A&C) or other deferential standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note's central proposal: de novo review is mandated by the APA’s text, structure, objectives, and administrative-deference principles; de novo review promotes predictability, constrains abuse, and allows courts to test agency justifications against the record (examples: D.C. Circuit in Ross and Sixth Circuit in Cain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Against applying arbitrary-and-capricious deference to good cause findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the A&C standard to agency claims of good cause gives agencies excessive latitude and lets them avoid notice-and-comment by providing minimal, conclusory rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deferential review may validate unsupported invocations and allow 'ad hoc' inconsistent results across circuits; courts should resist substituting deference for independent evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial application guidance: test rationales against the record
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying de novo review, courts should independently evaluate agency justifications, examine whether Congress’s framework undercuts urgency claims, and check agency behavior (delays, contemporaneous explanation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical factors for courts: the nature of statutory deadlines, whether the agency created the emergency, the strength of asserted harms from notice, scope/limitation of the rule, whether notice would be meaningless, and whether postpromulgation process occurred. Courts should articulate why the record does or does not support good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review should weigh competing interests: public participation and deliberation, agency flexibility, public safety, and judicial administrability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudication must account for these tradeoffs; de novo review does not demand rigidity—courts can preserve necessary flexibility while preventing routine circumvention of APA procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical administrability for courts
rubrics_metrics.description: De novo review should be workable—courts can apply familiar fact-intensive review techniques (analogous to de novo review of lower-court factual findings) to evaluate good cause assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note argues that although the inquiry will be fact-intensive and imperfectly enumerated, adopting a consistent nondeferential standard will increase predictability and reduce doctrinal confusion across circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-based indicators that undercut good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific record features that undermine good cause include agency delay in acting, lack of contemporaneous justification, existence of reliance interests, statutory text indicating expected delay, and absence of evidence that notice would produce harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should point to these indicators when rejecting good cause findings; the SORNA litigation examples illustrate these record-based analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of political-branch oversight as alternative remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Amending the statute or relying on Congress or the Executive to police good cause use is unlikely or undesirable; thus courts are the principal institutional check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because amendment has proven unrealistic and political monitoring is limited, judicial enforcement becomes the primary mechanism to ensure compliance—this institutional context supports a stronger judicial review standard.
